rationale: A better-resourced resident composition can support greater collective political influence.
scope: Neighborhood composition; not an effect of prices on incumbent income.

rationale: Effective resident influence can attract and shape investment in the focal neighborhood.
scope: Allocation may favor already influential groups; investment is not intrinsically equitable.

rationale: Sustained strain can reduce the capacity to organize and influence local decisions.
scope: Aggregate influence falls only where stressed priority residents form the relevant organizing base; influential newcomers can weaken this link.

rationale: Greater household resources can buffer persistent financial and residential strain.
Spending directed to usable public spaces can improve their quality for priority residents.
scope: Assumes implementation, maintenance and effective priority-group access.

rationale: Implemented service investment can improve affordable, appropriate local provision.
scope: Provision must address actual access barriers, not facility counts alone.

rationale: Transport spending can improve usable public transport when affordability and accessibility are specified.
scope: Requires inclusive service design and operating support.

rationale: Allocated street investment can deliver safer and more accessible active-travel routes.
Targeted housing programs can finance healthier homes for underserved residents.
scope: Assumes quality gains reach original priority residents and preserve affordability.

rationale: Targeted retrofit programs can improve energy performance in priority households' homes.
scope: With appropriate ventilation, installation and financial support.

rationale: Organized resident influence may help secure enforceable affordability and anti-displacement measures.
scope: Political translation is contingent, not guaranteed.

rationale: An operational equity response can redirect resources to underserved needs.
scope: Requires monitoring, mandate, budget, coordination and implementation.

rationale: An operational response can fund and enforce affordable housing protection.
scope: This is a proposed intervention response, not an observed automatic feedback.

rationale: A detected widening of unmet-needs disparities may trigger stronger equity action.
scope: MODEL ASSUMPTION: institutions detect the gap and are willing and able to respond.

rationale: Recognized unfair health gaps may increase the case for equity-oriented intervention.
scope: MODEL ASSUMPTION: evidence is translated into action; politics can weaken or block this link.

rationale: A worsening injury burden among priority residents may prompt an equity-focused safety response.
scope: MODEL ASSUMPTION: surveillance identifies the burden and decision makers act.

rationale: Effective affordability measures can reduce tenure-cost pressure on protected households.
scope: Refers to realized protective coverage, not any policy bearing an affordability label.

rationale: Secure affordable provision and enforceable tenure safeguards can reduce insecurity.
Effective protections can help original residents remain through neighborhood change.
scope: Coverage, enforcement, eligibility and housing supply matter.

rationale: Improved dwellings may become more desirable and command higher market costs.
scope: Market capitalization is weaker where affordability is permanently protected.

rationale: Better shared green amenities can increase nearby housing demand and market costs.
scope: Contextual capitalization; benefits can be retained with safeguards.

rationale: Market-valued amenity improvements accompanying better effective access may raise housing costs.
scope: Only where effective access accompanies market-valued amenity improvements. Affordability-only or accessibility-only changes need not raise prices.

rationale: Higher entry and retention costs can select a wealthier neighborhood resident composition.
scope: COMPOSITIONAL SORTING ONLY: original residents are not assumed to gain income; protections can interrupt sorting.

rationale: At unchanged household resources, higher rents or tenure payments increase cost burden.
scope: Exposed renters and purchasers; not every owner-occupier or protected tenancy.

rationale: Market-led upgrading can increase rents and purchase prices.
scope: Magnitude and timing vary across markets and tenures.

rationale: Neighborhood replacement processes may lead to forced moves among vulnerable original residents.
scope: Displacement is possible, not inevitable; tenure safeguards moderate the link.

rationale: Commercial replacement can reduce access to locally appropriate affordable services for original residents.
scope: Effective affordable access can fall even when aggregate amenity counts rise.

rationale: Persistent tenure-cost strain can undermine confidence in retaining adequate housing.
Higher housing cost burden can intensify chronic financial strain.
Uncertain housing security can sustain psychological strain.
Unaffordable tenure costs can compel original residents to move.
scope: Conditional on resources, protections, arrears processes and available alternatives.

rationale: Forced moves can break established support networks and local collective capacity.
scope: Follows original residents rather than improved neighborhood-average composition.

rationale: Disruption and lost residential control can increase persistent strain.
Household resources expand the feasible set of healthy homes and maintenance choices.
scope: Structural exclusion, market supply and discrimination may block this pathway.

rationale: Reduced damp, pollutants and other housing hazards can reduce physical morbidity.
scope: Housing quality is multidimensional; no universal magnitude is asserted.

rationale: Improved energy performance can reduce required energy expenditure for adequate comfort.
scope: Assumes service needs, tariffs, ventilation and financing costs do not offset savings.

rationale: A larger required energy-cost share can intensify chronic household financial strain.
Welcoming, well-maintained shared places can enable inclusive social encounters.
Inclusive collective capacity can support shared-space stewardship and upkeep.
scope: Requires usable resident influence and maintenance opportunities.

rationale: Collective efficacy and informal stewardship can reduce neglect and disorder.
Visible disorder can reduce feelings of neighborhood safety.
Feeling safe can support public-space use and neighborly interaction.
Perceived safety can increase willingness to walk, cycle and be active outdoors.
Usable green space can provide opportunities for stress recovery.
Vegetation and shade can reduce harmful heat experienced in shared places.
scope: Depends on actual canopy, design, use and local climate; public-space access is not a universal cooling proxy.

rationale: Accessible pleasant open spaces can support outdoor physical activity.
Connected nearby destinations can make walking and active trips more feasible.
Proximate connected destinations can reduce the need for private motorized trips.
scope: Mode substitution requires suitable services and feasible alternatives.

rationale: Complementary uses can sustain street presence and informal surveillance.
scope: A contextual mechanism; density alone is not assigned a universal safety effect.

rationale: Usable public transport can substitute for otherwise necessary car travel.
scope: Assumes mode substitution rather than exclusively additional journeys.

rationale: Affordable accessible transport can enable social journeys and reduce exclusion.
Safe, accessible routes and crossings can make active travel more feasible.
Protective street design and speed management can reduce population injury burden.
scope: At comparable travel exposure; induced activity is represented separately.

rationale: More time walking or cycling can increase exposure to road danger when infrastructure is unsafe.
scope: CONDITIONAL COUNTERPATH: population injury risk, not per-trip risk. Safety-in-numbers and safer infrastructure can weaken or reverse the net relationship.

rationale: Experienced or visible road danger may lower perceived safety of local travel.
scope: Risk perception is not identical to objectively measured injury risk.

rationale: Greater reliance on private motorized trips tends to add vehicle traffic.
scope: Traffic also reflects through journeys, occupancy and freight.

rationale: Additional vehicle traffic can increase pollutant emissions and local exposure.
scope: Depends on fleet, dispersion, proximity, routes and other sources.

rationale: Motor traffic is a source of harmful environmental noise.
scope: Vehicle speeds, barriers, fleet and building design moderate exposure.

rationale: Greater motor traffic can increase conflict exposure for vulnerable road users.
scope: Road design, speed and pedestrian/cyclist exposure held in context.

rationale: Pollutant exposure can contribute to respiratory and cardiovascular morbidity.
Persistent noise can disturb sleep and activate stress responses.
Harmful heat can increase acute illness and aggravate existing physical disease.
scope: Vulnerability and access to cooling modify effects.

rationale: Physical activity can reduce chronic physical disease risk.
scope: Not a promise of net benefit in every high-pollution or unsafe setting.

rationale: Prolonged stress may contribute to cumulative physical disease pathways.
scope: A coarse synthesis, not a quantified stress–disease coefficient.

rationale: Persistent stress can contribute to adverse mental health.
scope: Stress and clinical mental ill health are distinct constructs.

rationale: Inclusive support networks can buffer persistent psychosocial strain.
Physical morbidity may reduce capacity to obtain and sustain paid work.
scope: UNTESTED CLOSURE: the source identifies productivity as an evidence gap; disability inclusion, employment protections and illness severity matter.

rationale: Sustained paid work can increase household financial resources.
scope: MODEL ASSUMPTION: wage income is not fully offset by lost transfers or other expenses.

rationale: Mental ill health may reduce sustainable work participation.
scope: UNTESTED CLOSURE: do not infer causality from the reviewed unemployment-to-distress association.

rationale: Closing priority residents' healthy-housing shortfall can narrow the shelter-needs gap.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Removing priority residents' effective service-access barriers can narrow the access gap.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Meeting underserved groups' transport requirements can narrow unmet mobility needs.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Accessible safe routes can narrow underserved groups' mobility and safety shortfalls.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Disproportionately worsening housing insecurity can widen unmet shelter needs.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Disproportionate harmful heat exposure can widen unmet health-protection needs.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Improving priority groups' felt ability to use places safely can narrow the safety-needs gap.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Disproportionately worsening avoidable physical morbidity can widen the unfair health gap.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.

rationale: Disproportionately worsening avoidable mental morbidity can widen the unfair health gap.
scope: CONDITIONAL ACCOUNTING: the priority group's change must exceed the reference group's change; needs are assessed relative to group-specific requirements. No scalar weights or effect sizes are assumed.
